arXiv:2610.06260v1 [cs.CV] 05 Oct 2026

CentriQ: Calibration-Free Quantization of Diffusion Transformers via Exact Mean Centering

Nataša Jovanović Affiliation:  Tenstorrent Affiliation:  EPFL    Mathieu Salzmann Affiliation:  EPFL    Saqib Javed Affiliation:  EPFL
Abstract

Diffusion transformers (DiTs) achieve state-of-the-art image generation, but their sampling cost limits deployment. Quantizing both weights and activations to 4 bits reduces this cost, yet existing methods fall short in one of two ways. Calibration-based methods are tied to a specific checkpoint and prompt distribution, whereas data-free Hadamard rotation, effective for LLMs, loses quality on DiTs. We show that this loss has a structural cause. Adaptive layer-norm conditioning adds a per-token mean to the activations, and at the widths of the evaluated DiTs, the Hadamard rotations used by data-free methods cannot spread this mean uniformly across coordinates. A single dominant direction therefore survives the rotation and sets the quantization range. We introduce CentriQ, a calibration-free quantizer that centers each token before rotation and restores the mean exactly through a rank-1 full-precision branch, so that per-token scales follow in closed form without data. Weights are fitted under a robust ℓp\ell_{p} objective that tracks the dense mode of each group and discounts heavy tails. Across three DiTs, CentriQ matches the quality of calibrated SVDQuant at 4 bits, whereas calibration-free weight quantizers with plain per-token activation quantization collapse or degrade substantially. CentriQ outperforms the strongest calibration-free method reported to date at 2-bit weights. It is also the first calibration-free method to retain usable image quality at 2-bit activations.

1 Introduction

Diffusion transformers (DiTs) (Peebles and Xie, 2023) underlie state-of-the-art text-to-image models, but sampling them is expensive. Each image requires many denoising steps, and each step is dominated by the linear layers of the transformer blocks. Unlike autoregressive LLM decoding, which at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, a DiT forward pass is compute-bound. Weight-only quantization (e.g. W4A16) therefore reduces memory but not latency, because the low-bit weights are upcast to 16 bits before the matrix multiply, so activations must be quantized as well.

The post-training methods that do reach W4A4 on diffusion models all rely on calibration. A prompt set is run through the model to fit smoothing factors, clipping ranges, rotations, or error-compensating weight updates to the activation statistics of that specific model. SVDQuant (Li et al., 2025), for instance, migrates activation outliers into the weights using smoothing factors computed from COCO caption prompts, absorbs the magnified weight outliers in a 16-bit low-rank branch, and in its final version also applies GPTQ to the residual.

Calibration has costs beyond its compute budget. It makes the quantized model depend on a dataset, it must be repeated for every model, fine-tune, and quantization configuration, and its quality depends on how well the calibration prompts and timesteps match the deployment distribution. Calibration-free methods that reach four-bit activations on image DiTs have appeared only recently (Sec. 2), and they evaluate on generation benchmarks that do not measure fidelity to the full-precision model.

Two properties of DiT activations make the calibration-free setting difficult. First, adaptive layer normalization shifts and rescales every token with conditioning-dependent parameters, so each activation vector carries a per-token mean. A normalized Hadamard rotation, the standard tool for spreading outliers, maps this component onto one or a few coordinates, and the resulting outlier sets the quantization range for the whole vector. Second, only regular Hadamard matrices, whose rows have equal sums, spread this component uniformly, and these exist only at orders n=4​u2n=4u^{2}. None of the hidden widths of PixArt-Σ\Sigma (1152), FLUX.1 (3072), and SANA-1.6B (2240) has this form, so rotation methods operate through block-structured or Kronecker constructions, which inherit the mean problem.

We present CentriQ, a calibration-free W4A4 post-training quantization method for DiTs that addresses both properties directly. It subtracts the per-token mean before rotation, quantizes only the residual, and restores the mean exactly as a rank-1 term in the layer output, so the quantization range no longer depends on the offset. The centered activation is rotated by a deterministic factorized Hadamard matrix, and weights are quantized to grouped INT4 under a robust ℓp\ell_{p} (p<1p<1) objective, so neither path uses calibration data.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We show that adaLN places a per-token mean in DiT activations, which a Hadamard rotation concentrates onto one or a few coordinates that set the quantization range (Figs. 1 and 2).

  • •

    We show that after centering, the rotated operand, its per-token scale, and its quantization error contain no term that depends on the row sums of the rotation (Sec. 4.2, App. C.5). The choice of rotation is thereby decoupled from the mean, so CentriQ mixes globally with factorized Hadamard matrices and restores the mean exactly as a rank-1 term in the GEMM epilogue.

  • •

    CentriQ uses no calibration data and reaches FID and ImageReward that match calibration-based methods at W4A4 on three DiT families. Furthermore, it surpasses the strongest reported calibration-free method at W2A4 and is the first calibration-free method to hold image quality at W4A2 (Tab. 1, Tab. 4, Tab. 5).

Our code and models will be made publicly available.

2 Related work

PTQ for diffusion models.

Work on U-Net diffusion models showed that activation statistics drift with the timestep (Li et al., 2023; Shang et al., 2023; He et al., 2023; So et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024). Methods for diffusion transformers inherit this diagnosis and absorb the drift with calibration: PTQ4DiT (Wu et al., 2024) weights salient channels by timestep, Q-DiT (Chen et al., 2025) and ViDiT-Q (Zhao et al., 2025) use dynamic per-timestep or per-token activation scales, DiTAS (Dong and Zhang, 2025) aggregates smoothing factors across timesteps, LRQ-DiT (Yang et al., 2025) chooses rotations per layer from a calibrated metric, and AdaTSQ (Zhang et al., 2026) allocates bit-widths along the trajectory with Fisher-weighted Hessian calibration. The fitted statistics belong to one checkpoint and sampler, so these methods must be refit when the model or guidance changes. Sampler-side corrections (He et al., 2023; Ryu et al., 2026) act after quantization and are complementary to any quantizer, whereas training-based approaches (He et al., 2024; Sui et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026) fall outside the post-training setting.

Rotation and incoherence.

LLM quantization spreads activation outliers across channels by rotating the residual stream, with random orthogonal matrices in QuIP (Chee et al., 2023), randomized Hadamard transforms in QuIP# (Tseng et al., 2024), and Hadamard rotations folded into the weights in QuaRot (Ashkboos et al., 2024b). Learned rotations (Liu et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025) recover accuracy that a fixed Hadamard loses, but they are fit on calibration data. All of these assume a Hadamard matrix of the model width, which the Sylvester construction gives only for powers of two, so other widths use a Kronecker product H2k⊗HmH_{2^{k}}\otimes H_{m} with a small hand-picked HmH_{m}.

Mean removal.

SliceGPT (Ashkboos et al., 2024a) and QuaRot fold LayerNorm mean subtraction into the preceding weights, which is exact in LLMs. In a DiT, the adaLN modulation depends on the timestep and prompt and makes the mean vary per token, so this static fold does not apply. HadaNorm (Federici et al., 2025) subtracts a per-channel mean computed over tokens at inference and applies SmoothQuant-style per-channel scales, fitted on a calibration set, before a Hadamard transform, and reports W4A4 on PixArt-Σ\Sigma. CentriQ removes the per-token mean instead and requires no calibration data. To our knowledge, no public implementation of HadaNorm is available, which precludes a direct comparison under our protocol. ConvRot (Huang et al., 2025) spreads the mean with group-wise regular Hadamard transforms of order 4k4^{k}, which mix only within each group, whereas CentriQ removes the mean and mixes globally with factorized Hadamard matrices.

Calibrated W4A4 for DiTs.

SVDQuant (Li et al., 2025) was the first to reach reasonable 4-bit weights and activations on image DiTs, by keeping a low-rank branch in 16 bits after SmoothQuant-style migration (Xiao et al., 2023) fit on captioned images, with fused kernels in Nunchaku. DiRotQ (Sharify et al., 2026) preserves a calibration-derived PCA subspace of the activations at higher precision and quantizes weights with GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023), improving over SVDQuant on PixArt-Σ\Sigma under the MJHQ-30K protocol, which is not directly comparable with the MJHQ-5k protocol used here. HQ-DiT (Liu and Zhang, 2024) reaches 4-bit operands with a floating-point grid.

Calibration-free quantizers.

On the weight side, RTN, NF4 (Dettmers et al., 2023), HQQ (Badri and Shaji, 2023), and SINQ (Müller et al., 2026) operate on the weight tensor alone. NF4 assumes near-Gaussian weights, HQQ fits the dense mode under an ℓp\ell_{p} objective with p<1p<1, and SINQ balances a second scale axis with Sinkhorn iterations. Calibration-free 4-bit activations on DiTs are recent. DVD-Quant (Li et al., 2026) achieves W4A4 for video DiTs with grid refinement, rotated quantization, and adaptive bit switching. ConvRot achieves it on FLUX-family models with group-wise rotation, NVFP4 weights, and per-tensor FP8 activation scales. OrbitQuant (Lee et al., 2026) quantizes weights and activations in a randomly permuted block-Hadamard basis with a Lloyd–Max codebook derived from the post-rotation marginal (Zandieh et al., 2026), and reports GenEval on FLUX.1 and Z-Image-Turbo down to W2A4. Neither image method removes the token mean, both mix within blocks whose order divides the width, and both evaluate on generation benchmarks that do not measure fidelity to the full-precision model.

Position of this work.

CentriQ is calibration-free on both axes and produces integer W4A4 operands for every transformer-block projection. We evaluate it on PixArt-Σ\Sigma, FLUX.1-schnell, and SANA-1.6B with FID, ImageReward, LPIPS, and PSNR against the 16-bit reference on MJHQ, and compare against the published results of calibrated SVDQuant. To our knowledge it is the first calibration-free integer W4A4 method evaluated for fidelity across three image-DiT architecture families.

3 Preliminaries

A linear layer computes 𝐲t=W​𝐱t+𝐛\mathbf{y}_{t}=W\mathbf{x}_{t}+\mathbf{b}, where W∈ℝdout×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times n} and 𝐱t∈ℝn\mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the activation of token tt. We write 𝟏\mathbf{1} for the all-ones vector, ∥⋅∥∞\|\cdot\|_{\infty} for the largest coordinate magnitude, and a hat for a quantized tensor.

Quantizers.

Activations are quantized online to a symmetric bb-bit grid with one 16-bit scale per token.

Qa​(𝐱t)=αt⋅clip⁡(round⁡(𝐱t/αt),−(2b−1−1), 2b−1−1),αt=rt2b−1−1,Q_{a}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\alpha_{t}\cdot\mathrm{clip}\!\big(\mathrm{round}(\mathbf{x}_{t}/\alpha_{t}),\,-(2^{b-1}-1),\,2^{b-1}-1\big),\qquad\alpha_{t}=\frac{r_{t}}{2^{b-1}-1}, (1)

where the range rtr_{t} is either ‖𝐱t‖∞\|\mathbf{x}_{t}\|_{\infty} or a high percentile of |𝐱t||\mathbf{x}_{t}|, computed from the current token at inference. Because one scale serves all nn coordinates, a single large coordinate coarsens the grid for the whole token. Weights are quantized to an asymmetric bb-bit grid over groups of gg consecutive input columns,

W^g=𝝈⁡(Qg−𝐳),Qg∈{0,…,2b−1}dout×g,\widehat{W}_{g}=\bm{\sigma}\,(Q_{g}-\mathbf{z}),\qquad Q_{g}\in\{0,\dots,2^{b}-1\}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times g}, (2)

with a per-(row, group) scale 𝝈\bm{\sigma} and shift 𝐳\mathbf{z} stored in 16 bits. Round-to-nearest (RTN) sets both from the group minimum and maximum, an ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} criterion, and an ℓ2\ell_{2}-optimal scale is likewise dominated by the largest entries of the group, which motivates the criterion of Sec. 4.3.

Hadamard rotation.

A Hadamard matrix Hn∈{±1}n×nH_{n}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n\times n} satisfies Hn​Hn⊤=n​IH_{n}H_{n}^{\top}=nI, so H=1n​HnH=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}H_{n} is orthogonal and can be folded into the weight without changing the layer, W​𝐱=(W​H⊤)​(H​𝐱)W\mathbf{x}=(WH^{\top})(H\mathbf{x}). Hadamard matrices exist at every order 2k2^{k} (Sylvester), at q+1q+1 for a prime power q≡3(mod4)q\equiv 3\pmod{4} (Paley type I), and at 2​(q+1)2(q+1) for q≡1(mod4)q\equiv 1\pmod{4} (Paley type II), and the Kronecker product Ha⊗HbH_{a}\otimes H_{b} is Hadamard of order a​bab. Each coordinate of H​𝐱H\mathbf{x} is a signed sum 1n∑j±xj\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{j}\pm x_{j}, so the rotation spreads a coordinate outlier over all nn outputs and shrinks rtr_{t} in Eq. (1) (Ashkboos et al., 2024b; Tseng et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). A component along 𝟏\mathbf{1} is the exception, since Hn​𝟏H_{n}\mathbf{1} is the vector of row sums of HnH_{n} and spreads that component uniformly only when all row sums are equal. Hadamard matrices with equal row sums are called regular (Seberry and Yamada, 1992).

Lemma 1 (Regular Hadamard matrices).

If all row sums of a Hadamard matrix HnH_{n} with n>1n>1 equal cc, then n=4​u2n=4u^{2} and c=±2​uc=\pm 2u for an integer uu. The Sylvester matrix H2kH_{2^{k}} is not regular for k≥1k\geq 1, and Ha⊗HbH_{a}\otimes H_{b} is regular only if both factors are (proof in App. C.5).

4 Method

4.1 Motivation: DC energy in DiT activations

The DC component and its origin.

For a token 𝐱t∈ℝn\mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with channel mean x¯t=1n​𝟏⊤​𝐱t\bar{x}_{t}=\tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{t}, we call x¯t​𝟏\bar{x}_{t}\mathbf{1} its DC component and measure its share of the token energy by

fDC​(t)=n​x¯t2‖𝐱t‖22∈[0,1].f_{\mathrm{DC}}(t)=\frac{n\,\bar{x}_{t}^{2}}{\|\mathbf{x}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}}\in[0,1]. (3)

In a DiT block, the QKV and first MLP projections receive the adaLN output 𝐱t=(1+𝜸)⊙𝐱~t+𝜷\mathbf{x}_{t}=(1+\bm{\gamma})\odot\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t}+\bm{\beta}, where 𝐱~t\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t} is the LayerNorm output and the conditioning vectors (𝜸,𝜷)(\bm{\gamma},\bm{\beta}), which depend on the timestep and prompt, are shared by all tokens. Because 𝐱~t\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t} has zero channel mean, the modulation reintroduces one, x¯t=β¯+1n​𝜸⊤​𝐱~t\bar{x}_{t}=\bar{\beta}+\tfrac{1}{n}\bm{\gamma}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t} with β¯=1n​𝟏⊤​𝜷\bar{\beta}=\tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\bm{\beta}, whose second term varies per token and therefore cannot be folded into a bias. The second MLP projection receives post-activation features, which also have a nonzero mean. Accordingly, fDCf_{\mathrm{DC}} is nonzero on the modulated input, whereas on the LayerNorm output it stays at the floor set by storage precision (Fig. 1, top).

Rotation does not remove it.

Because H​PHP preserves norms (PP zero-pads to width n′n^{\prime}, Sec. 4.2), the DC component keeps its energy n​x¯t2n\bar{x}_{t}^{2} after rotation and maps to x¯t​H​P​𝟏\bar{x}_{t}\,HP\mathbf{1}, whose coordinates are the row sums of H​PHP. For a factorized rotation H=(Hm⊗H2k)/n′H=(H_{m}\otimes H_{2^{k}})/\sqrt{n^{\prime}} (Sec. 4.2), the Sylvester factor sends 𝟏\mathbf{1} onto its first coordinate, so at least a fraction n/n′n/n^{\prime} of this energy falls on mm coordinates, and all of it when 2k2^{k} divides nn. A power-of-two rotation (m=1m=1) therefore places it in a single coordinate of magnitude |x¯t|​n/n′|\bar{x}_{t}|\,n/\sqrt{n^{\prime}}. Uniform spreading requires a regular Hadamard matrix (Lemma 1). Even then it shifts every coordinate by ±x¯t\pm\bar{x}_{t}, so the range still grows with |x¯t||\bar{x}_{t}|.

Consequence for 4-bit activations.

The per-token step Δt∝maxj⁡|(H​P​𝐱t)j|\Delta_{t}\propto\max_{j}|(HP\mathbf{x}_{t})_{j}| is then set by the DC coordinate, so the incoherent bulk of the token is quantized on a grid sized for the DC spike. Consistent with this, rotation alone leaves the per-token max/RMS\max/\mathrm{RMS} ratio at the level of the unrotated token, whereas centering before rotation lowers it to the level that incoherence predicts for the centered part (Fig. 1, bottom).

4.2 Activation path

Centering and exact re-injection.

Each token is centered over its nn native channels, 𝐱tc=𝐱t−x¯t​𝟏\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}=\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{x}_{t}\mathbf{1}, at a cost of O⁡(n)O(n) per token and one scalar stored alongside the per-token scale, and the fused kernel of App. B.2 computes the mean in the same launch as the range. Because the layer is linear, the removed component re-enters the output exactly through a rank-1 term,

W​𝐱t=W​𝐱tc+x¯t​𝐰𝟏,𝐰𝟏=W​𝟏∈ℝdout.W\mathbf{x}_{t}=W\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}+\bar{x}_{t}\,\mathbf{w}_{\mathbf{1}},\qquad\mathbf{w}_{\mathbf{1}}=W\mathbf{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}}. (4)

The row-sum vector 𝐰𝟏\mathbf{w}_{\mathbf{1}} is computed once in FP32 from the unquantized weight and stored at the model’s compute precision, so the DC component bypasses both quantizers.

Rotation.

The centered token is rotated by a fixed orthogonal matrix H=(Hm⊗H2k)/n′H=(H_{m}\otimes H_{2^{k}})/\sqrt{n^{\prime}} of order n′=m​ 2k≥nn^{\prime}=m\,2^{k}\geq n, where H2kH_{2^{k}} is a Sylvester matrix and HmH_{m} is a Paley matrix of order m∈{12,36,44}m\in\{12,36,44\} or m=1m=1. When nn factors in this form, the rotation runs at the native width, and otherwise PP zero-pads the token to the smallest admissible n′n^{\prime}. The factorization applies the rotation as two small transforms in O⁡(n′​(m+2k))O(n^{\prime}(m+2^{k})) operations per token. Because centering precedes padding, 𝟏n′⊤​P​𝐱tc=0\mathbf{1}_{n^{\prime}}^{\top}P\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}=0 and the padded lanes are exactly zero, so the DC component is absent from the rotated token for every admissible n′n^{\prime}, whatever the row sums of HH (Fig. 2).

Scale and grid.

The rotated token H​P​𝐱tcHP\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c} is quantized to a symmetric bb-bit grid with one scale per token. We estimate its spread as σ^t\hat{\sigma}_{t}, the empirical ρ\rho-quantile of the magnitudes |(H​P​𝐱tc)j||(HP\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c})_{j}| divided by the half-normal quantile Φ−1​((1+ρ)/2)\Phi^{-1}((1+\rho)/2), and set αt=γ⋆​σ^t/(2b−1−1)\alpha_{t}=\gamma^{\star}\hat{\sigma}_{t}/(2^{b-1}-1), where γ⋆=2.56\gamma^{\star}=2.56 minimizes the combined clipping and rounding error of a 4-bit grid for Gaussian input (Banner et al., 2019). Both ρ=0.9995\rho=0.9995 and γ⋆\gamma^{\star} are fixed across models and layers, and σ^t\hat{\sigma}_{t} and x¯t\bar{x}_{t} are computed on the current token at inference.

Forward pass.

One quantized linear layer computes

𝐲t=W^R​Qa​(H​P​𝐱tc)+x¯t​𝐰𝟏+𝐛,W^R≈W​P⊤​H⊤∈ℝdout×n′,\mathbf{y}_{t}=\widehat{W}_{R}\,Q_{a}\!\big(HP\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}\big)+\bar{x}_{t}\,\mathbf{w}_{\mathbf{1}}+\mathbf{b},\qquad\widehat{W}_{R}\approx WP^{\top}H^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times n^{\prime}}, (5)

where the first term multiplies the 4-bit rotated weight of Sec. 4.3 with the 4-bit rotated token, and the rank-1 term and bias are fused into the epilogue of this matrix multiplication at compute precision (App. B.2).

Offset invariance.

Centering turns the DC component into an exact rank-1 term, so the quantized layer of Eq. (5) satisfies

𝐲⁡(𝐱t+c​𝟏)=𝐲⁡(𝐱t)+c​𝐰𝟏for every ​c∈ℝ,\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}_{t}+c\mathbf{1})=\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+c\,\mathbf{w}_{\mathbf{1}}\qquad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb{R}, (6)

and its deviation from W​𝐱t+𝐛W\mathbf{x}_{t}+\mathbf{b} depends on 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} only through 𝐱tc\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}. The scale, the codes, and the quantization error therefore contain no terms that depend on the row sums of HH, so the rotation can be chosen for mixing and width alone.

4.3 Weight path

The weight quantizer operates offline on the rotated weight WR=W​P⊤​H⊤∈ℝdout×n′W_{R}=WP^{\top}H^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times n^{\prime}}, split into groups WgW_{g} of g=64g=64 consecutive input columns. Row ii of group gg reconstructs as si​σi​g​(Qi​g−zi​g)s_{i}\,\sigma_{ig}\,(Q_{ig}-z_{ig}), with 4-bit codes QgQ_{g}, a per-(row, group) scale 𝝈g\bm{\sigma}_{g} fixed at its min/max initialization, a per-(row, group) shift 𝐳g\mathbf{z}_{g}, and a per-row scale 𝐬\mathbf{s} shared across the groups of a row. Since si​σi​gs_{i}\sigma_{ig} is folded into a single 16-bit scale at export, the stored format matches Eq. (2). The codes and the remaining parameters solve

min⁡∑g𝐬,𝐳,Q⁡‖Wg−diag⁡(𝐬)​[(Qg−𝐳g)⊙𝝈g]‖pp,p=0.7,Qg∈{0,…,15}dout×g,\min_{\mathbf{s},\,\mathbf{z},\,Q}\ \sum_{g}\big\|W_{g}-\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{s})\,\big[(Q_{g}-\mathbf{z}_{g})\odot\bm{\sigma}_{g}\big]\big\|_{p}^{p},\qquad p=0.7,\quad Q_{g}\in\{0,\dots,15\}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times g}, (7)

where ‖E‖pp=∑i​j|Ei​j|p\|E\|_{p}^{p}=\sum_{ij}|E_{ij}|^{p}. We call this weight quantizer RoDS and fix pp and gg across models and layers.

Why a robust ℓp\ell_{p} objective.

Min/max scaling, the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} criterion of RTN, and ℓ2\ell_{2} scale fits both let the largest entries of a group set the scale (Sec. 3). Under ℓp\ell_{p} with p<1p<1, the marginal cost p​|r|p−1p|r|^{p-1} of a residual decreases with |r||r|, so a few large entries are fitted poorly at small cost while the dense mode of the group sets the scale. Since DiT weight groups are heavy-tailed, a min/max scale stretches the grid over the tail and wastes resolution on the mode, whereas the ℓp\ell_{p} fit resolves the mode. Tab. 7 compares the ℓp\ell_{p} fit with min/max scaling (RTN), NF4, and HQQ.

Solver.

We solve the nonconvex, nonsmooth problem in Eq. (7) by nested alternation. The outer loop fits 𝐬\mathbf{s} with the codes and shifts frozen. Because the residual is linear in 𝐬\mathbf{s}, each row reduces to an ℓp\ell_{p} regression, which we solve by iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) with weights (ϵ+ri​j2)(p−2)/2(\epsilon+r_{ij}^{2})^{(p-2)/2} on the current residuals. The inner loop refits (𝐳g,Qg)(\mathbf{z}_{g},Q_{g}) on the preconditioned tile Wg/𝐬W_{g}/\mathbf{s} by half-quadratic splitting, where an auxiliary residual EgE_{g} decouples the ℓp\ell_{p} term from the reconstruction,

min⁡∑g𝐳,Q,E⁡(‖Eg‖pp+β2​‖Eg−(Wg/𝐬−(Qg−𝐳g)⊙𝝈g)‖F2).\min_{\mathbf{z},\,Q,\,E}\ \sum_{g}\Big(\|E_{g}\|_{p}^{p}+\frac{\beta}{2}\,\big\|E_{g}-\big(W_{g}/\mathbf{s}-(Q_{g}-\mathbf{z}_{g})\odot\bm{\sigma}_{g}\big)\big\|_{F}^{2}\Big). (8)

Each inner iteration rounds the scaled target Wg/(𝐬​𝝈g)+𝐳gW_{g}/(\mathbf{s}\,\bm{\sigma}_{g})+\mathbf{z}_{g} to the grid, shrinks EgE_{g} with the generalized shrinkage of HQQ (Badri and Shaji, 2023) as a one-step approximation of the proximal operator of ∥⋅∥pp\|\cdot\|_{p}^{p}, and sets 𝐳g\mathbf{z}_{g} in closed form as the per-row mean offset between the codes and the residual-corrected target. Since 𝐬\mathbf{s} is initialized to 𝟏\mathbf{1} and 𝝈g\bm{\sigma}_{g} stays at its min/max initialization, the first inner iteration coincides with RTN, and 𝐬\mathbf{s} is the only scale fitted under ℓp\ell_{p}. The penalty β\beta is fixed, and the iteration counts and tolerances are listed in App. B.3.

5 Results

We evaluate CentriQ on PixArt-Σ\Sigma, SANA-1.6B, and FLUX.1-schnell at 102421024^{2} resolution, using MJHQ-5k and sDCI following the SVDQuant protocol, plus GenEval on FLUX.1-schnell. All methods are run with identical prompts, seeds, and metric code, and design choices were made on a disjoint development split. Full details of models, samplers, metrics, baselines, and hardware are given in Appendix A.

Tab. 1 compares W4A4 methods on PixArt-Σ\Sigma, FLUX.1-schnell, and SANA-1.6B. Without calibration, CentriQ matches calibrated SVDQuant: relative to each method’s 16-bit reference, FID and ImageReward are comparable on all three models, and CentriQ attains the lowest LPIPS. On SANA-1.6B, CentriQ stays within 0.2 FID of the BF16 model on both benchmarks. SVDQuant attains a higher PSNR on PixArt-Σ\Sigma and SANA-1.6B, whereas CentriQ attains a lower LPIPS, which weights perceptual structure over pixel-wise intensity. Both methods reach an FID below their 16-bit reference on FLUX.1-schnell, which lies within the noise of FID at 5k samples (Chong and Forsyth, 2020).

RTN, NF4, and HQQ collapse on PixArt-Σ\Sigma and degrade substantially on FLUX.1-schnell and SANA-1.6B, so among the evaluated methods CentriQ is the only calibration-free one that produces usable images on all three models. CentriQ achieves this with the same grouped 4-bit weight format as RTN and HQQ.

Fig. 4 compares SVDQuant and CentriQ on GenEval prompts at W4A4, W4A2, and W2A4, and Figs. 12, 13, and 14 in the appendix compare them at W4A4 on all three models. All images in a row share the prompt, seed, scheduler, and step count, which is the same seed-level pairing that underlies the fidelity metrics in Tab. 1.

5.1 Latency results

We measure the latency of CentriQ at W4A4 on FLUX.1-schnell on a single A100-80GB GPU at 1024×\times1024 resolution and 44 denoising steps. The deployed model uses a single-pass activation quantization kernel together with Nunchaku’s 4-bit GEMMs. CentriQ generates an image in 1.69 s, whereas the BF16 model takes 1.77 s. The full calibration-free pipeline therefore runs slightly faster than the unquantized model as the time saved by the 4-bit matrix multiplication covers the cost of the added operations.

6 Ablations

Tab. 2 adds rotation, centering with exact re-injection, and percentile clipping one at a time to a baseline that uses the grouped ℓp\ell_{p} weight quantizer and per-token activation quantization without any transform. The rotation-only row corresponds to a QuaRot-style data-free Hadamard rotation. Centering lowers FID from 25.65 to 18.46 at W4A4 and from 35.84 to 21.81 at W2A4. Percentile clipping is decisive at W4A2, where it lowers FID from 444.21 to 35.59, and changes W4A4 FID by 0.34, so a single clip setting serves all three bit-widths.

7 Discussion and limitations

The per-token mean that CentriQ removes originates in the adaLN modulation, which all three conditioning designs share, so one activation path transfers across PixArt-Σ\Sigma, FLUX.1-schnell, and SANA-1.6B without per-model tuning. By Lemma 1, none of the evaluated DiT widths admits a rotation that spreads this component uniformly, which makes explicit mean removal the direct remedy for Hadamard-based activation quantization in these models. Because the centered, rotated token contains no term that depends on the row sums of the rotation (Eq. (10), App. C.5), a single clip percentile, fixed once for all models and layers, reaches the quality of calibrated SVDQuant in Tab. 1.

Limitations.

The 2-bit configurations are evaluated on FLUX.1-schnell with simulated quantization, because no fused kernel yet supports 2-bit activations. Latency is measured on A100 integer tensor cores, and transferring CentriQ to the microscaling FP4 formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) of newer GPUs remains to be evaluated. The analysis targets DiTs conditioned through adaLN, which covers the three evaluated families, and the gain from centering is expected to be smaller in architectures whose activations carry little per-token mean.

8 Conclusion

We showed that adaptive layer normalization places a per-token mean in DiT activations, which a Hadamard rotation concentrates onto a few coordinates that dominate the quantization range. CentriQ centers each token before rotation and restores the mean exactly through a rank-1 term, which makes the quantization range independent of the rotation, and it quantizes weights under a robust ℓp\ell_{p} objective, so no step requires calibration data. At W4A4, CentriQ matches calibrated SVDQuant on all three models, and its centering and rotation add no net latency over BF16 inference. On FLUX.1-schnell, it also retains usable image quality at W2A4 and extends calibration-free quantization to 2-bit activations. A fused kernel for 2-bit activations and an extension to video diffusion transformers are natural next steps.

Appendix A Experimental setup

Models.

We evaluate CentriQ on PixArt-Σ\Sigma, SANA-1.6B and FLUX.1-schnell. The three models use different attention designs (full self-attention, linear attention, and joint text-image attention in an MM-DiT), and each injects conditioning through adaLN shift terms, which produce the per-token mean that centering removes. All three generate 102421024^{2} images: PixArt-Σ\Sigma and SANA-1.6B sample with 20 steps of DPM-Solver and Flow-DPM-Solver, respectively, at a guidance scale of 4.5, whereas FLUX.1-schnell samples with 4 flow-matching Euler steps at a guidance scale of 0.

Benchmarks.

Following the SVDQuant protocol, we generate one image per prompt for the 5,000 prompts of MJHQ-5k and the 5,000 prompts of sDCI. Each prompt has a fixed seed that all methods share, so the paired metrics compare outputs generated from the same initial noise. On FLUX.1-schnell, we additionally report GenEval, which scores compositional prompts using an object detector on 553 prompts with four images per prompt. All configuration choices, including the rotation layout and the clip percentile, were made on a disjoint 1,000-prompt development split of MJHQ. The evaluation split was scored once per final configuration, so no reported number informed a design decision.

Metrics.

FID and ImageReward measure image quality, with FID computed against the benchmark’s reference images. PSNR and LPIPS measure fidelity to the 16-bit model by comparing each quantized output with the 16-bit output for the same prompt and seed. Both are computed on decoded 8-bit RGB images, and PSNR uses a peak value of 255.

Baselines.

We run RTN, NF4, and HQQ in our harness with identical prompts, seeds, and metric code, and in their rows of Tab. 1 activations are quantized per token without a transform. For Tab. 1, we report SVDQuant from Li et al. (2025), whose MJHQ-5k and sDCI protocol we follow. For GenEval and the qualitative figures, we run SVDQuant from the Nunchaku wheel with smoothing factors calibrated on COCO captions, as in the original work.

Hardware and kernels.

All generation and latency measurements run on a single NVIDIA A100-80GB GPU. The 4-bit GEMMs use Nunchaku, which we extend with the centering and rotation operations. We measure end-to-end latency on FLUX.1-schnell, including the text encoders and the VAE decoder, with CUDA events as the mean over 6 images after 2 warm-up runs. Configurations below 4 bits for weights or activations use simulated quantization because no fused kernel supports these formats, so all latency figures refer to 4-bit weights and activations.

Appendix B Implementation details

B.1 Rotation construction

CentriQ rotates each activation-quantized input with the factorized Hadamard matrix H=(Hm⊗H2k)/n′H=(H_{m}\otimes H_{2^{k}})/\sqrt{n^{\prime}} of order n′=m​ 2kn^{\prime}=m\,2^{k}, where H2kH_{2^{k}} is the Sylvester matrix and HmH_{m} is a tabulated matrix with m∈{1,12,36,44}m\in\{1,12,36,44\} (H36H_{36} Paley type II, H44H_{44} Paley type I). When the native width nn admits such a factorization, the rotation runs at n′=nn^{\prime}=n, and otherwise the centered token is zero-padded by P=[In; 0]P=[I_{n};\,0] to the smallest admissible n′>nn^{\prime}>n. The weight absorbs H⊤H^{\top} offline as W​P⊤​H⊤WP^{\top}H^{\top}, so the layer output is unchanged, and all matrices are deterministic. The Kronecker structure (Hm⊗H2k)​vec​(X)=vec⁡(H2k​X​Hm⊤)(H_{m}\otimes H_{2^{k}})\,\mathrm{vec}(X)=\mathrm{vec}(H_{2^{k}}XH_{m}^{\top}), with the token reshaped to X∈ℝ2k×mX\in\mathbb{R}^{2^{k}\times m}, reduces the transform from n′2n^{\prime 2} to n′​(m+2k)n^{\prime}(m+2^{k}) multiply-adds.

The factorization also explains why centering must precede the rotation. At the native width, the Sylvester factor maps 𝟏2k\mathbf{1}_{2^{k}} onto its first coordinate, so H​𝟏n=2k/m​(Hm​𝟏m)⊗𝐞1H\mathbf{1}_{n}=\sqrt{2^{k}/m}\,(H_{m}\mathbf{1}_{m})\otimes\mathbf{e}_{1} and the offset x¯t​𝟏n\bar{x}_{t}\mathbf{1}_{n} lands with its full energy n​x¯t2n\bar{x}_{t}^{2} on at most mm of the n′n^{\prime} coordinates. Removing the per-token mean over the nn native coordinates eliminates this spike exactly, whereas centering after padding would leave a fraction (n′−n)/n′(n^{\prime}-n)/n^{\prime} of the offset energy in the operand.

B.2 Fused kernel

The W4A4 GEMM extends the INT4 kernels of Nunchaku on an A100-SXM4-80GB and evaluates

𝐲^t=W~​Qa​(H​P​𝐱tc)+x¯t​𝐫+𝐛,𝐫=W​𝟏n,\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t}=\widetilde{W}\,Q_{a}\!\left(HP\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}\right)+\bar{x}_{t}\,\mathbf{r}+\mathbf{b},\qquad\mathbf{r}=W\mathbf{1}_{n}, (9)

with W~=QW​(W​P⊤​H⊤)\widetilde{W}=Q_{W}(WP^{\top}H^{\top}) and 𝐫\mathbf{r} precomputed from the full-precision weight in FP32. The prologue loads each token tile once, subtracts its mean, applies the factorized HH as tensor-core products, and quantizes to {−7,…,7}\{-7,\dots,7\} with one scale per token. Since weight codes are stored as Q−8Q-8 with zero point z′=z−8z^{\prime}=z-8, the asymmetric grid leaves a correction C=s​z′C=sz^{\prime} per row and 64-channel group. Nunchaku’s low-rank side branch absorbs this correction together with the rank-1 term and the bias through the activation columns [αt​𝐩t​∣x¯t∣​1][\,\alpha_{t}\mathbf{p}_{t}\mid\bar{x}_{t}\mid 1\,] and weight columns [−C​∣𝐫∣​𝐛][\,-C\mid\mathbf{r}\mid\mathbf{b}\,], where 𝐩t\mathbf{p}_{t} holds the group sums of the activation codes, so the integer main product is unchanged.

On FLUX.1-schnell (102421024^{2}, 4 steps, batch 1), the native factorization lets the CUDA-graphed W4A4 transformer run without padding, and the full pipeline takes 1.69 s per image (Sec. 5.1). The W4A2 configurations use simulated quantization and carry no latency claim.

B.3 Solver settings

The weight quantizer fits asymmetric 4-bit groups of 64 input channels in the rotated basis, with 16-bit scale and zero point in the model precision (4.5 bits per weight). Starting from the HQQ min-max initialization, the solver alternates IRLS updates of the per-row scale with half-quadratic splitting updates of the codes and zero point, while the group scale stays at its min-max value. Activations use a symmetric per-token grid whose scale follows a Gaussian model: σ^t=q0.9995​(|H​P​𝐱tc|)/Φ−1​(0.99975)\hat{\sigma}_{t}=q_{0.9995}(\lvert HP\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}\rvert)/\Phi^{-1}(0.99975) and αt=γ⋆​σ^t/(2b−1−1)\alpha_{t}=\gamma^{\star}\hat{\sigma}_{t}/(2^{b-1}-1). Tab. 3 lists all settings, shared across models and layers.

Appendix C Additional results

C.1 Sub-4-bit

Tab. 4 reports the corresponding fidelity metrics at sub-4-bit precision on FLUX.1-schnell. At W4A2, FID increases relative to W4A4, yet CentriQ keeps a positive ImageReward without any calibration data, which agrees with the compositional accuracy it retains in Tab. 5.

C.2 GenEval

Fidelity metrics measure agreement with the 16-bit output, not whether the quantized model still follows the prompt. We therefore evaluate compositional generation on FLUX.1-schnell with GenEval (Tab. 5). For completeness, the table also includes results reported by the concurrent preprint OrbitQuant (Lee et al., 2026). At W4A4, CentriQ preserves prompt adherence: its Overall score of 0.670 matches BF16 (0.667) and is close to our calibrated SVDQuant reproduction (0.682), although OrbitQuant and AdaTSQ score higher. Below four bits, the comparison favors CentriQ. At W2A4, the rotation and smoothing baselines collapse to near-zero scores, whereas CentriQ reaches 0.647, ahead of OrbitQuant (0.604) on every sub-task except Colors. At W4A2, CentriQ retains 0.573 and is the only calibration-free method reported in this regime. Because W2A4 outperforms W4A2 on every sub-task, activation precision limits compositional quality more than weight precision does, which supports the emphasis of Sec. 4 on the activation quantizer.

C.3 Activation path ablations

Tab. 6 fixes the CentriQ activation path and varies the weight quantizer. With the activation path in place, all four quantizers produce usable images on FLUX.1-schnell and SANA-1.6B, where they collapse or degrade substantially without it (Tab. 1). On PixArt-Σ\Sigma, RoDS further lowers FID from 21.04 (HQQ) to 19.13.

C.4 Weight path ablations

Tab. 7 isolates the weight quantizer by keeping activations at 16 bits. At W3A16, the ℓp\ell_{p} quantizer attains the lowest FID on all three models, and the margin is largest on PixArt-Σ\Sigma, where it lowers FID from 34.36 (HQQ) to 29.04. ImageReward follows FID on PixArt-Σ\Sigma and FLUX.1-schnell. At W4A16, the four quantizers stay within 0.4 FID of each other on FLUX.1-schnell and SANA-1.6B, whereas on PixArt-Σ\Sigma the ℓp\ell_{p} quantizer and HQQ lead RTN and NF4 by more than 2 FID.

C.5 Analysis

The forward pass in Eq. (5) contains two approximations, the weight quantizer W^R\widehat{W}_{R} and the activation quantizer QaQ_{a}, and one exact rewriting, the rank-1 branch. We first verify that the rewriting is exact, then show what centering removes from the range that QaQ_{a} has to cover.

Exactness of the re-injection.

The decomposition in Eq. (4) is an algebraic identity in WW and 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}, because 𝐱tc+x¯t​𝟏=𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}+\bar{x}_{t}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{x}_{t} and 𝐰𝟏=W​𝟏\mathbf{w}_{\mathbf{1}}=W\mathbf{1} by definition. Setting W^R=W​P⊤​H⊤\widehat{W}_{R}=WP^{\top}H^{\top} and Qa=idQ_{a}=\mathrm{id} in Eq. (5) therefore recovers W​𝐱t+𝐛W\mathbf{x}_{t}+\mathbf{b} exactly, since P⊤​H⊤​H​P=InP^{\top}H^{\top}HP=I_{n}. In finite-precision arithmetic the branch adds one rank-1 update in the epilogue, with 𝐰𝟏\mathbf{w}_{\mathbf{1}} stored at the model’s compute precision. Consequently every deviation of CentriQ from the full-precision model is attributable to W^R\widehat{W}_{R} and QaQ_{a}, whereas the branch carrying the DC component contributes none.

What centering removes from the range.

Because H​PHP is linear, the rotated token splits as

H​P​𝐱t=H​P​𝐱tc+x¯t​H​P​𝟏,HP\mathbf{x}_{t}=HP\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}+\bar{x}_{t}\,HP\mathbf{1}, (10)

where H​P​𝟏HP\mathbf{1} is the vector of row sums of H​PHP. The second term concentrates at least a fraction n/n′n/n^{\prime} of the DC energy on mm coordinates, one of which has magnitude at least |x¯t|​n/m​n′|\bar{x}_{t}|\,n/\sqrt{mn^{\prime}}, so without centering it lower-bounds the per-token range whenever the centered part does not cancel it, and Fig. 2 shows that it dominates the range in practice. Since the per-token step Δt\Delta_{t} is proportional to the range, this single coordinate coarsens the grid for all n′n^{\prime} coordinates of the token. Centering makes the second term identically zero, and since the padding is zero-padding applied after centering, 𝟏n′⊤​P​𝐱tc=0\mathbf{1}_{n^{\prime}}^{\top}P\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}=0 holds at the rotation’s width. The rotated centered token H​P​𝐱tcHP\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c} therefore contains no term that depends on the row sums of HH, and the same holds for every quantity computed from it: the absmax range, the percentile scale of Sec. 4.2, the quantized codes, and the quantization error. This is an identity for every token and every timestep and requires no distributional assumption. By Lemma 1, no Hadamard matrix at the native hidden widths of the evaluated models has constant row sums, so without centering the row-sum term is present for every one of them, whereas with centering the rotation can be selected for mixing quality and width alone.

How small the remaining range ‖H​P​𝐱tc‖∞\|HP\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}\|_{\infty} is depends on the centered token and on the mixing of the rotation. Under sub-Gaussian coordinates of 𝐱tc\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c} it concentrates at O⁡(log⁡n′​‖𝐱tc‖2/n′)O\!\big(\sqrt{\log n^{\prime}}\,\|\mathbf{x}_{t}^{c}\|_{2}/\sqrt{n^{\prime}}\big), so the per-token max/RMS\max/\mathrm{RMS} ratio of the rotated centered token grows only as O⁡(log⁡n′)O(\sqrt{\log n^{\prime}}), consistent with the centering + rotation curves in Fig. 1 (bottom).

Proof of Lemma 1.

If Hn​𝟏=c​𝟏H_{n}\mathbf{1}=c\mathbf{1}, then c2​n=‖Hn​𝟏‖22=𝟏⊤​Hn⊤​Hn​𝟏=n2c^{2}n=\|H_{n}\mathbf{1}\|_{2}^{2}=\mathbf{1}^{\top}H_{n}^{\top}H_{n}\mathbf{1}=n^{2}, so c2=nc^{2}=n. No Hadamard matrix of order 2 has this property because 2 is not a square, and every Hadamard order n>2n>2 is divisible by 4, so a square order satisfies n=4​u2n=4u^{2} with c=±2​uc=\pm 2u. One row of H2kH_{2^{k}} sums to 2k2^{k} and every other row sums to zero, so H2kH_{2^{k}} is not regular for k≥1k\geq 1. The row sums of Ha⊗HbH_{a}\otimes H_{b} are the products si​tjs_{i}t_{j} of the row sums sis_{i} of HaH_{a} and tjt_{j} of HbH_{b}. If all products equal cc, then c≠0c\neq 0 by the first part, and fixing jj gives si=c/tjs_{i}=c/t_{j} for every ii, so all sis_{i} are equal, and the same argument shows that all tjt_{j} are equal.

AI use statement

We used large language models (LLMs) to edit the manuscript for grammar, wording, and consistency, and to check cross-references, table entries, and derivations for internal consistency. The authors reviewed and revised all AI-assisted text. We take full responsibility for the content of this work, including text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Reproducibility statement

The paper specifies every component needed to reimplement CentriQ. Sec. 4.2 and App. B.1 define the centering, the factorized Hadamard rotation, the padding rule, and the closed-form per-token scale, and Sec. 4.3 and App. B.3 give the ℓp\ell_{p} objective, the solver, and all hyperparameters, which are shared across models and layers (Tab. 3). App. B.2 describes how the rank-1 term and the zero-point correction are fused into the Nunchaku 4-bit GEMM. All models, prompt sets (MJHQ-5k, sDCI, GenEval), and metrics are public, and App. A lists the samplers, step counts, guidance scales, seeding protocol, and the Nunchaku release used for SVDQuant.

Ethics statement

CentriQ lowers the cost of running text-to-image models, which widens access for legitimate uses and for misuse alike. The quantized models inherit the safety behavior and biases of their 16-bit sources, and this work does not evaluate either. We collected no new data and ran no studies with human participants. All prompt sets come from public benchmarks and are used under their respective licenses.
